card.title: Vander Waals Forces, Molecular Solids and Hydrogen Bonding

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Between molecules, the forces are a ladder: **London dispersion** (universal, growing with electron count — the reason I₂ is solid and Cl₂ gaseous), **Debye** and **Keesom** dipole terms, and above them the **hydrogen bond** — X–H ⋯ Y where X and Y are small, electronegative F, O or N, worth 5–40 kJ mol⁻¹.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - H-bond energy: 5–40 kJ mol⁻¹ (vs O–H covalent 463) - Boiling points: H₂O 100, H₂S −60, HF 19.5, HCl −85, NH₃ −33, PH₃ −87.7 °C - Ice density 0.92 g cm⁻³ < water 1.00 - Halogen bp: F₂ −188, Cl₂ −34, Br₂ 59, I₂ 184 °C

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **H-bond strength vs covalent strength:** an H-bond is ~10× weaker than the O–H covalent bond (5–40 vs 463 kJ mol⁻¹) — boiling breaks H-bonds, not covalent bonds; water does not decompose at 100 °C.  ·  **"van der Waals" as umbrella:** the term covers dispersion + Debye + Keesom; the hydrogen bond is usually treated separately because it is far stronger and directional.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***DNA's zipper*** — A=T held by 2 H-bonds, G≡C by 3: weak individually, but thousands in sequence give a stable double helix that still unzips for replication — hydrogen bonding doing information storage.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Two anomalous-property generators: (1) H-bond count per molecule — water's four-connectivity beats HF's chains and NH₃'s lower donor capacity, which is why water's bp rise is the largest of the trio; (2) intramolecular H-bonds subtract from intermolecular association.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Intermolecular ladder: London dispersion (universal, ∝ polarisability/size) < Debye < Keesom < hydrogen bond (5–40 kJ mol⁻¹, X–H ⋯ Y with F/O/N). Molecular solids: soft, low mp, insulators (I₂, dry ice, naphthalene).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Gecko feet and the surface tension of water both trace to intermolecular attractions; capillary rise in soil and xylem is cohesion (H-bonds) plus adhesion.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Weak Forces That Hold Matter Together Covalent bonds build molecules; **intermolecular forces** decide whether those molecules are gas, liquid or solid. Weakest to strongest: London dispersion → Debye (dipole-induced) → Keesom (dipole-dipole) → hydrogen bond.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 van der Waals forces — the three tiers - **London dispersion forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole):** electron clouds flicker; a momentary dipole induces one in the neighbour. Present in **all** molecules; the *only* force in nonpolar ones (N₂, noble gases).…  ·  ## 3. Comparison Tables **Intermolecular forces ranked** | Force | Between | Relative strength | Example | |---|---|---|---| | London dispersion | All molecules | Weakest (grows with size) | I₂ solid, N₂ liquid at 77 K | | Debye | Permanent + nonpolar | Weak | HCl ⋯ Ar | | Keesom | Two permanent dipoles | Weak | HCl ⋯…  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **Hydrogen bonding needs F, O, N — not just any H:** C–H hydrogens are barely positive (C EN 2.5); CH₄ cannot hydrogen-bond. Chlorine, though EN 3.0, is too large for the close approach — HCl's "H-bond" is negligible.  ·  **Intramolecular H-bonds lower, not raise, boiling points:** the bond is spent inside the molecule, leaving less for intermolecular association (o- vs p-nitrophenol).
